stem:
You are assessing a 9-year-old boy after a severe temper outburst. These have occurred more than once, the most recent resulting in an emergency department visit. His parents describe him as argumentative and highly oppositional at home, and he has had several suspensions from school for swearing and fighting. His mother is finding him unmanageable.

He meets diagnostic criteria for oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). He is considered intellectually able but is inattentive and is not doing well at school.

Which one of the following interventions has the potential to make the most difference in the short term?

options.text: Individual therapy focusing on anger management
Moving him to a specialised school for children with behavioural disorders
Training the parents in behaviour management strategies

explanation: In children with ODD, the most effective short-term intervention is usually parent behaviour management training. It helps carers respond consistently, reduce coercive cycles, and improve day-to-day behaviour. Because this child is also inattentive and underperforming at school, ADHD should be assessed, but immediate management of the oppositional behaviour is most likely to improve functioning quickly.
rationale: ODD is managed first with behavioural and family-based interventions. Parent training has the strongest evidence for near-term benefit and directly addresses oppositional behaviour in the home setting. Stimulants may be helpful if comorbid ADHD is contributing, but they do not replace parent management strategies.

optionExplanations.A: May help with emotional regulation, but is usually less immediately effective than parent-focused behaviour management.
optionExplanations.B: Specialised schooling may be considered in severe cases, but it is not the most effective short-term intervention here.
optionExplanations.C: Can be useful as an adjunct, but is not the intervention most likely to produce rapid improvement in ODD.
optionExplanations.D: Stimulants may help if ADHD is present, but they are not the primary short-term treatment for ODD itself.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Parent behaviour management training is the intervention most likely to improve ODD symptoms in the short term.

You are assessing a 9 year old boy who has presented to your medical practice following a massive temper outburst. These have occurred on more than one occasion, the most recent one resulting in a visit to the emergency department of his local hospital. On questioning his parents you discover that he is argumentative and highly oppositional at home and has had several suspensions from school for swearing and fighting. His mother is finding him unmanageable.

You find that he meets the diagnostic criteria for oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). He is considered intellectually able but is inattentive and is not doing well at school.

Which one of the following interventions has the potential to make the most difference in the short term?
